stories.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 and opens 34% higher on Nasdaq
stories.plain: Anthropic sold shares to the public for the first time, at $83 each, above the range it had marketed. The stock started trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT and opened at $111.50.
stories.eng: The deal was upsized to 980 million Class A shares, almost all sold by Anthropic itself, with a 30-day option for underwriters to buy 147 million more. Alongside it, seven companies (Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC) bought $26 billion of separate non-trading Class N stock at the same price. Founders keep a fixed 50.1% of the vote through a Class F share.
stories.point: The point: the first frontier lab to list publicly raised more than any IPO before it, and its own chip and cloud suppliers bought in at the same price.
stories.means: Until now, frontier labs were funded only by private rounds, so their finances were mostly hidden. Going public means quarterly reports, audited numbers and a share price that moves daily. The amended filing showed Q3 revenue of $16.96 billion with a $567 million operating loss, and roughly $900 billion of compute commitments. The big strategic placement matters because it ties the companies that sell Anthropic chips and cloud capacity directly to its share price.
stories.industry: The listing beats SpaceX's June IPO as the largest ever and gives public investors a direct way to bet on a frontier lab, which will set a reference price for OpenAI and others. It also brings more scrutiny: four senators introduced a bill the same week requiring public companies to disclose more about AI. Watch whether the stock holds as quarterly numbers and compute bills arrive.
stories.you: Expect Anthropic's pricing, rate limits and roadmap to be shaped partly by quarterly earnings now, the way cloud providers' are. Public filings will also give you real data on serving costs and margins, which helps when you estimate what model APIs will cost in a year.
terms: Greenshoe
An option letting underwriters sell up to ~15% more shares after an IPO if demand is strong.
Fully diluted
Share count including options and unvested stock, used for the higher valuation figure.
stories.why: The first-day close was reported at $97.17, up 17% from the offer price, and the stock fell further in Friday's broad AI selloff.
stories.source: ZeroHedge · 19 Nov; The Next Web · 18 Nov; CNBC (via AI Frontier Daily) · 20 Nov

stories.title: Anthropic mathematician claims Riemann proof with Claude, in Lean
stories.plain: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a statement saying he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics. No independent expert has confirmed it yet.
stories.eng: Instead of a human-readable paper, Alpöge released a formalization in Lean, a proof assistant that mechanically checks each step, split into 14 archive parts. He says the arguments were formalized without extra assumptions and that the method also covers the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. He calls the argument very long and says he has not yet fully mastered the mathematics it uses.
stories.point: The point: if the Lean files check out and state the right theorem, this would be the first major open problem settled with a machine-checked proof largely produced by an AI.
stories.means: The Riemann Hypothesis predicts how prime numbers are spread out; it has resisted proof for 167 years and carries a $1 million prize. Many claimed proofs have failed. Lean changes the question: a computer can confirm every step follows, but experts still have to confirm two things, that the hypothesis is stated correctly in the code and that no hidden assumptions slipped in. Scientific American noted those two checks are exactly what mathematicians will now examine. In August, Claude had already improved a 50-year-old partial bound on the problem, from 41.6% to 67.2% of zeros.
stories.industry: Labs have been pushing 'AI that proves things' because machine-checked output can be trusted without a human reading every line. A confirmed result would be the strongest evidence yet that agents can do original frontier research, not just engineering. A failed one would still show how hard it is to verify a formal statement matches what you meant.
stories.you: The lesson for code is the same: a passing proof or test only covers what the spec says. When you use agents with formal checks (types, property tests, Lean or Dafny), review the spec itself as carefully as you would review code.
terms: Lean
A programming language and proof assistant that checks each step of a mathematical proof by computer.
Formalization
Rewriting a proof so every step is machine-checkable.
stories.why: Scientific American separately reported dueling claims of Riemann proofs emerging.
stories.source: Scientific American (via Digg) · 20 Nov; Anthropic · 10 Aug

stories.title: Meta FAIR agent writes its own memory rules, then trains them in
stories.plain: Meta researchers let an AI agent design its own rules for what to save and recall between tasks, then baked those habits into the model's weights. The self-written rules beat the best ones humans wrote.
stories.eng: The task agent's only memory is a folder of files; two prompts control it, OFFLOAD (what to save after a task) and LOAD (what to read before the next). A meta-agent reads the task agent's runs, finds memory failures and rewrites those prompts, keeping the best-scoring versions. Then the team swaps generic prompts back into the recorded good runs and fine-tunes Kimi-K2.6 on them with a rank-64 LoRA, so the model behaves well even without the special prompts.
stories.point: The point: memory strategy for agents can be searched for automatically and then distilled into weights, instead of hand-written per task.
stories.means: Agents forget everything between sessions unless you give them a memory system, and writing good rules for what to remember is guesswork; the team found no single hand-written design won on every task. Here the model searches for its own rules and gets a clear jump, especially on the codebase task. Distillation keeps part of the gain (roughly a third, by one outside estimate) without the prompts. The search is noisy: most rewrites made things worse, and results cover one benchmark, three tasks and one model.
stories.industry: Continual learning, getting better after deployment without full retraining, is a major open problem for agents. This is a practical recipe: optimize the harness, then compress it into a cheap LoRA adapter. It fits the broader move to treat prompts and harnesses as things to optimize, not hand-tune.
stories.you: If you run agents with file-based memory, treat your save and load instructions as a parameter to optimize against an eval, not a fixed prompt. Even without fine-tuning, an automated rewrite-and-score loop over those two prompts is cheap to try.
terms: LoRA
Low-rank adaptation: training a small add-on matrix instead of the full model's weights.
Harness distillation
Fine-tuning a model on runs that used special prompts so it behaves that way without them.
stories.why: Base model was Kimi-K2.6, a 1-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 32B active parameters.
stories.source: Meta FAIR (via FourWeekMBA) · 17 Nov; MarkTechPost (via Rio Rundown) · 19 Nov

stories.title: Google opens Genie 4 world model to subscribers and the Gemini API
stories.plain: Google DeepMind's Genie 4, which generates explorable 3D worlds you can walk through in real time, became available to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie. A day later it reached developers through the Gemini API.
stories.eng: Genie 4 is a transformer that takes text, images and live keyboard and mouse input and generates video frame by frame with synchronized audio, built on Gemini Omni Flash with Gemini used for steering. Users can change the world mid-session by text prompt, such as the weather or characters. Google gave no quantitative evaluations and lists long-term consistency and complex physics as open problems.
stories.point: The point: an interactive world model is now an API call, so developers can test it as a simulator, not just watch demos.
stories.means: A world model learns how scenes behave over time so it can predict the next frame given an action, much like a game engine that was learned rather than coded. Genie 3 sessions ran about a minute; Genie 4 doubles that and adds sound. Two minutes is still short and scenes can drift, so this is a research tool, not a replacement for a physics engine.
stories.industry: World models are the main bet for training robots and agents in simulation, where mistakes are free; DeepMind has already used Gemini with Genie 4 as a robot practice environment. AMD's purchase of World Labs last week shows hardware companies want in too.
stories.you: If you work on agents, games or robotics, you can now prototype against a generated environment without building one. Treat outputs as plausible, not physically accurate, and keep episodes short.
terms: World model
A model that predicts how an environment changes in response to actions.
Drift
Gradual loss of consistency as generated scenes run longer.
stories.why: Each output carries a SynthID watermark.
stories.source: Google DeepMind model card · 18 Nov; Google (via AI Frontier Daily) · 18–19 Nov; The Batch · 6 Nov

stories.title: OpenAI's Codex agents now hunt and fix ChatGPT slowdowns
stories.plain: OpenAI described an internal system where its Codex coding agents investigate when ChatGPT gets slower, propose fixes and check that speed recovers after the fix ships. It has run over 1,700 investigations in about three months.
stories.eng: When monitoring detects a latency regression, agents are triggered to run profilers, compare before-and-after profiles, find the cause and propose a patch, then verify recovery in production. OpenAI's performance team has described a second, proactive loop where specialized agents search in parallel for latency, CPU, memory, bundle-size and database savings. Its stated preconditions are good tests, reliable benchmarks, observability and safe rollout.
stories.point: The point: agents are moving from writing features to running production operations work on a system with hundreds of millions of users.
stories.means: Performance work is slow and repetitive: someone notices a slowdown, bisects changes, profiles, and fixes. At ChatGPT's scale, many small regressions land every week and humans can't chase all of them. Handing the first pass to agents, with automatic checks that the fix worked, turns it into a pipeline. OpenAI's team has warned that if benchmark or deploy cycles take hours, agents add little.
stories.industry: Labs increasingly point to their own infrastructure being maintained by agents as evidence that AI speeds up AI. It also shows where the leverage is: not in the model alone, but in the profilers, benchmarks and rollout tooling the agent can call.
stories.you: Before handing regressions to agents, make your perf signals agent-friendly: reproducible benchmarks, profiles you can diff, and fast canaries. A good first project is a bot that bisects and profiles a regression and posts a diagnosis for a human to approve.
terms: Regression
A change that makes something slower or worse than before.
Canary
Rolling a change out to a small share of traffic first to catch problems.
stories.why: Digests differ on wording: one says 600+ cases resolved, the other 600+ root causes found.
stories.source: OpenAI (via Rio Rundown and The Neuron) · 20 Nov; ZenML LLMOps database

stories.title: Gemini can now operate your Mac; Apple is building its own agent
stories.plain: Google's Gemini app for Mac can now use native apps, local files and websites on its own in the background. The same day, Bloomberg reported Apple is building its own computer-using agent and will warn users about giving full access to others.
stories.eng: Gemini runs actions while showing a live preview, and the user can pause, stop or approve steps; Google's examples are filling forms, batch-renaming files, sorting folders and building slides from dashboards. Apple posted a job for a manager to build an agent that can use a computer, and per Bloomberg, macOS 27.3 will add warnings before granting third-party agents full access.
stories.point: The point: computer-use agents are reaching the desktop OS, and the platform owner is starting to gate access to it.
stories.means: Computer-use agents look at the screen and click and type like a person, which lets them work with apps that have no API. Until now these mostly ran in browsers or sandboxes. Running in the background on a real Mac means the agent can touch any local file or app, which is useful and risky. Apple said in October it would require very explicit user action for that access, and the new warnings are the first concrete step.
stories.industry: Every major lab now ships a desktop agent, and OS vendors control the permission layer they all depend on. If Apple builds its own while adding friction for rivals, it repeats the pattern of app store and browser gatekeeping, now for agents.
stories.you: If you build desktop automation, plan for OS-level permission prompts and design for the user approving actions. Prefer scoped access, such as specific folders or apps, over full disk and accessibility rights.
terms: Computer use
An AI model operating software through the screen, mouse and keyboard.
Accessibility permissions
OS rights that let one app read and control other apps' interfaces.
stories.why: Google also shipped Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API this week, which loads tool schemas on demand to cut input tokens.

stories.title: AWS lets AI agents buy software on their own, billed to the cloud
stories.plain: Amazon now lets companies authorize AI agents to buy software on AWS Marketplace without a human approving each purchase. Companies set budgets and rules for which purchases still need review.
stories.eng: Bedrock AgentCore can charge marketplace purchases to a company's AWS bill using the x402 payment protocol, with no stablecoin wallet needed. Charges arrive as asynchronous invoice line items at fixed quoted prices, and payment tokens expire after about five minutes. An optional AgentCore Gateway connector helps agents discover paid services.
stories.point: The point: a major cloud now gives agents a spending account with guardrails, which turns agent payments from demos into procurement.
stories.means: x402 revives the old HTTP 402 'Payment Required' code: a service tells the agent the price, the agent pays and retries. Most x402 demos used crypto wallets, which companies avoid. Billing through the existing cloud invoice removes that blocker. The short token lifetime and per-session and per-request caps limit how much a confused or hijacked agent can spend.
stories.industry: Agents that can pay for APIs, data and tools are a prerequisite for agents doing real work across companies. It comes the same week big US banks moved liability for agent actions onto customers, so the spending limits matter.
stories.you: If you build agents that call paid APIs, start designing around budgets and per-call caps now. If you sell an API, x402 support could make it reachable to agents without a sales process.
terms: A protocol that uses HTTP status 402 to let clients, including agents, pay per request.
AgentCore
AWS's managed runtime and tooling for deploying AI agents.
stories.why: AWS's marketplace VP Matt Yanchyshyn described the purchasing change to Fortune.
stories.source: Fortune (via Rio Rundown) · 20 Nov; AWS (via Superpower Daily) · 19 Nov

stories.title: Stanford's TRACER watches ICU video to flag early delirium
stories.plain: A Stanford team built an AI system that combines round-the-clock bedside video with medical records to track what ICU patients are doing and spot signs of delirium. Patients who tested positive for delirium showed much less purposeful activity in the system's records.
stories.eng: TRACER is training-free: vision models turn video into minute-level action logs, which are merged with clinical records into hourly reports. An LLM agent gets tools to query that hierarchy, pull up relevant video and fetch records to answer clinicians' questions. Because nothing is trained, no protected health data goes into model weights.
stories.point: The point: an agent with tools over video and records can give nurses continuous observation that no staff schedule allows.
stories.means: Delirium, sudden confusion, is common in ICU patients and linked to lasting cognitive damage, but it is checked only a few times a day by short bedside tests. Continuous video could catch changes earlier. The design is notable: instead of training one big medical model, the team chains existing models and lets an agent query the results, which sidesteps privacy and data limits. The QA test is small, 144 questions from two patients, so this is early.
stories.industry: Healthcare is a test case for agents built from off-the-shelf models plus domain tools. It also shows the privacy pattern regulators prefer: data is queried at runtime, not baked into weights. UC Health said the same week it will add ChatGPT to medical-record software and expand AI phone agents.
stories.you: The 'logs, then summaries, then an agent with query tools' pattern works for any long video or telemetry stream. It is cheaper and easier to audit than fine-tuning, and each answer can point back to the source clip.
terms: Training-free
Built from existing models without training new weights on the target data.
Delirium
An acute state of confusion common in hospitalized patients.
stories.why: Authors include Zane Durante, Paul Tang, Ehsan Adeli, Arnold Milstein and Fei-Fei Li.
stories.source: Stanford HAI (via Rio Rundown) · 20 Nov; arXiv 2610.21266 · 15 Oct

stories.title: AI is now designing quantum error-correction codes and decoders
stories.plain: An industry analysis this week laid out how AI tools are taking over a core quantum job: designing the codes that protect fragile qubits and the decoders that fix errors. Several groups report AI-found designs that beat the best human ones.
stories.eng: IBM's OpenEvolve uses an LLM inside an evolutionary loop to propose and test code designs. QC Design's Meridian searched over 100 fault-tolerance design tasks. On decoding, DeepMind's AlphaQubit is a transformer, and NVIDIA's Ising decoders are 3D convolutional networks; NVIDIA separately released a CUDA-Q decoder said to cut design-research compute from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.
specs: Up to 2.5x faster, 3x more accurate than PyMatching
stories.point: The point: error correction, the main barrier to useful quantum computers, is becoming a search problem that AI is good at.
stories.means: Qubits make errors constantly, so a useful quantum computer spreads each logical qubit across many physical ones and a classical decoder works out which errors happened, in real time. Newer qLDPC codes need fewer qubits than the classic surface code but are harder to design and decode. AI search finds better codes, and neural decoders read the error signals faster and more accurately. A lower logical error rate means fewer physical qubits per useful qubit, which pulls the timeline forward.
stories.industry: This is where AI and quantum meet in practice: GPUs sit next to quantum chips to run decoders, and LLM search designs the codes. NVIDIA, IBM and Google are all positioning their AI stacks as part of the quantum toolchain.
stories.you: Decoding is a tight-latency streaming inference problem, the same skills as real-time ML serving on GPUs and FPGAs. If you want into quantum, CUDA-Q and open decoders like PyMatching are the practical entry points.
terms: Logical qubit
An error-protected qubit built from many physical qubits.
Decoder
Classical software that infers which errors occurred from measurement data.
stories.why: Figures come from each company's own claims, compiled by Quantum Computing Report, not one shared benchmark.
stories.source: Quantum Computing Report · 19 Nov; NVIDIA · 16 Nov

stories.title: Oregon sues OpenAI for $2.035B, says ChatGPT misled on teen safety
stories.plain: Oregon's attorney general sued OpenAI, saying it marketed ChatGPT as safe for kids while knowing its protections for minors were weak. The state asks for at least $2.035 billion and stronger safeguards.
stories.eng: The 53-page complaint is brought under Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act, a consumer-protection law, and calls the violations willful. It says OpenAI often fails to confirm parental consent for 13–17-year-olds, that its 'ChatGPT for Teens' parent-linking can be bypassed, and that parents were not alerted when teens asked about suicide, self-harm or eating disorders.
stories.point: The point: states are using consumer-protection law, not new AI statutes, to hold chatbot makers to their safety claims.
stories.means: With no federal AI law, state attorneys general are suing under existing rules against deceptive marketing. The argument is not that AI is illegal, but that OpenAI said its product was safe for teens when it was not. Eight states sued in October on similar grounds, so a pattern is forming. Attorney General Dan Rayfield said no single Oregon incident triggered the suit. OpenAI said it keeps building safeguards like parental controls and break reminders.
stories.industry: If these cases succeed, every consumer AI product's safety claims become legal exposure. That pushes companies toward verifiable age checks and documented safeguards, and supports calls for one national standard instead of 50 state ones.
stories.you: If you ship a consumer AI feature, treat marketing claims about safety like a spec you can be sued over. Log and test safeguards such as age gates and crisis-topic handling, and make sure they cannot be bypassed trivially.
terms: Attorney general
A state's chief legal officer, who can sue companies on behalf of residents.
Unfair trade practices law
Consumer-protection law against deceptive or unfair business conduct.
stories.why: Separately, Congress saw the ROOT CAUSE Act introduced on 18 Nov, which would create a board to investigate major AI and cyber failures.

eras.name: Large language models
eras.short: Models trained to predict the next word turn out to write, translate and code.
eras.how: A transformer is trained on a large share of the public internet to predict the next token. Capabilities appear with scale: GPT-3 could do tasks it was never trained for, given a few examples in the prompt.
eras.built: Autocomplete, text generation APIs, early GitHub Copilot.
eras.broke: Raw models ramble, make things up and do not follow instructions reliably.

eras.name: Chatbots
eras.short: Instruction tuning and human feedback make models useful in a conversation.
eras.how: Fine-tune the base model on examples of good answers, then use reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) so it prefers helpful, safe replies.
eras.built: Chat interfaces, customer support bots, writing assistants.
eras.broke: The model only knows its training data and cannot look anything up or do anything.

eras.name: RAG and tool use
eras.short: Models get access to your documents and to APIs.
eras.how: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt. Function calling lets the model output a structured call to an API you define.
eras.broke: One question, one answer. Multi-step tasks still needed a human driving every step.

eras.name: Workflows
eras.short: Engineers chain model calls into fixed pipelines.
eras.how: You write the steps in code: classify, then retrieve, then draft, then check. The model fills in each step, but the control flow is yours.
eras.built: Document processing pipelines, LangChain-style chains, eval harnesses.
eras.broke: Fixed pipelines break on anything you did not anticipate. Real tasks need the system to decide what to do next.

eras.name: Agents
eras.short: The model decides the next step itself, in a loop with tools.
eras.how: A loop: the model looks at the goal and results so far, picks a tool, runs it, reads the output, repeats until done. Reasoning models that think before answering made these loops far more reliable.
eras.built: Coding agents, computer-use agents, MCP servers that expose tools to any agent.
eras.broke: Agents worked for minutes, then drifted, looped or lost track on long tasks.

eras.name: Autonomous agents
eras.short: Agents run for hours on real work in sandboxes, with little supervision.
eras.how: Better long-horizon training, sandboxed environments, checkpoints and the ability to run tests let an agent own a whole task: open the repo, make the change, run CI, open a pull request.
eras.built: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity; agents opening PRs while you sleep.
eras.broke: One agent is one thread of work. Large problems need many in parallel.

eras.name: Multi-agent orchestration
eras.short: A planner agent splits work across specialist agents.
eras.how: An orchestrator breaks a goal into subtasks, hands them to worker agents with different tools or prompts, and merges the results.
eras.built: Agent teams for research, code migration and analysis; orchestration frameworks.
eras.broke: Coordination overhead grows fast, and someone still has to check every worker’s output.

eras.name: Agent swarms with verifiers
eras.short: Hundreds to thousands of agents work against an automatic checker that accepts only correct results.
eras.how: Instead of trusting agents, you trust the verifier: a proof checker, test suite or simulator. Agents propose, the verifier filters, survivors get refined. Memory layers start letting agents keep what they learn.
eras.built: 1,000-agent formal proof of Fermat in ~30h; AI-designed quantum circuits beating human designs; Signal's crypto code verified by agents in Lean.
eras.broke: Still open: it only works where a strict automatic check exists.
eras.marks: Fermat formalization (9 Nov 2026), AI quantum circuits (10 Nov 2026), AlphaProof Code on Signal (10 Nov 2026)

eras.name: World models and continual learning
eras.short: Contenders for what comes next: models that learn physics from observation and keep learning after deployment.
eras.how: World models simulate how an environment will change when you act, which lets agents plan in the physical world. Continual learning updates the model from experience without retraining from scratch.
eras.built: Research prototypes, robotics simulation, NeurIPS 2026 workshops.
eras.broke: Not yet reliable outside labs. Watch Frontier for signals.
eras.marks: Genie, V-JEPA, Continual World Models workshop (NeurIPS 2026)
